RECITALS / WHEREAS:
A. The Borrower had availed a secured term loan of Rs. 7,70,00,000/-
(Rupees Seven Crores and Seventy Lakhs only) from the Bank on or about
05.09.2015 for purchase of a commercial property, repayable in 108 (one
hundred  and  eight)  Equated  Monthly  Instalments  commencing  from
05.10.2015, carrying interest at the rate of 13.5% per annum compounded
monthly, with penal interest of 2% per annum on default. The said loan
was secured, inter alia, by an equitable mortgage of the commercial
property created in favour of the Bank.
B. Upon the Borrower's account being classified as a Non-Performing Asset
on 05.05.2016, the Bank initiated proceedings under the Securitisation
and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security
Interest Act, 2002 (“SARFAESI Act”), including the issuance of a Demand
Notice dated 04.10.2016 under Section 13(2) and a Possession Notice
dated 26.12.2017 under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act.
C. The Borrower instituted S.A. No. 425 of 2019 before the Ld. Debts
Recovery Tribunal-II, Hyderabad (“DRT”), wherein I.A. No. 885 of 2023
came to be filed seeking reduction of the contractual rate of interest.
By Order dated 05.07.2023, the Ld. DRT directed that simple interest at
10% per annum be charged on the reduced balance.
D. Aggrieved, the Bank preferred Misc. Appeal No. 35 of 2023 before the
Ld. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal, Kolkata (“DRAT”), which by Order
dated 10.05.2024 set aside the Order of the Ld. DRT.
E. The Borrower thereafter filed W.P. No. 22458 of 2024 before the Hon'ble
High Court of Telangana at Hyderabad, which by judgment and Order dated
30.04.2025 set aside the Order of the Ld. DRAT and restored the Order
of the Ld. DRT dated 05.07.2023.
F. Aggrieved by the said judgment dated 30.04.2025, the Bank preferred
Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 24286 of 2025 (“SLP”) before the
Hon'ble  Supreme  Court  of  India,  which  is  presently  pending
adjudication. In the said proceedings, a sum of Rs. 1,25,00,000/-
(Rupees One Crore and Twenty-Five Lakhs only) has been deposited by the
Borrower with the Registry of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India.
G. Having regard to the predominantly commercial character of the disputes
between the Parties and with a view to amicable resolution, the
Parties, by mutual consent, referred the disputes to mediation. Hon'ble
Mr. Justice R. Subhash Reddy, former Judge of the Hon'ble Supreme Court
of India (hereinafter referred to as the “Ld. Mediator”), was appointed
as the Mediator to resolve the disputes under the aegis of mediation in
accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Mediation Act, 2023.

--- Page 205 ---
3
H. Pursuant to such appointment and reference, the mediation proceedings
were deemed to have commenced under Section 14 of the Mediation Act,
2023, and were conducted in due compliance with Sections 15 to 18 of
the said Act. After several rounds of joint and separate sessions held
between the Parties under the auspices of the Ld. Mediator, the Parties
have, of their own free will and volition, voluntarily and without any
coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, and with the
benefit of independent legal advice, arrived at a full and final
amicable settlement of all the disputes, differences and claims between
them on the terms and conditions hereinafter recorded.
I. The Parties confirm that this Settlement Agreement is reduced into
writing in accordance with Section 19(2) of the Mediation Act, 2023,
and shall, upon execution, be submitted to the Ld. Mediator for
authentication in terms of Section 19(3) of the said Act.
NOW, THEREFORE, IN CONSIDERATION OF THE MUTUAL COVENANTS AND PROMISES
HEREINAFTER CONTAINED, AND WITH A VIEW TO BURY ALL DIFFERENCES AND DISPUTES
BETWEEN THE PARTIES, THE PARTIES HEREBY AGREE, RECORD AND DECLARE AS FOLLOWS:
1. FULL AND FINAL SETTLEMENT AMOUNT  
1.1 In full and final settlement of all dues, claims, demands, interest
(contractual, pendente lite, future and penal), costs, charges and
expenses arising out of or in connection with the loan facility
referred to in Recital A above and the disputes set out in Recitals B
to F (collectively, the “Disputes”), the Borrower agrees to pay, and
the Bank agrees to accept, an aggregate sum of Rs. 15,75,00,000/-
(Rupees Fifteen Crores and Seventy-Five Lakhs only) (the “Settlement
Amount”).
2. MODE AND SCHEDULE OF PAYMENT  
2.1 The Settlement Amount shall be paid by the Borrower to the Bank in the
following manner:
a) Release of Deposit with the Supreme Court Registry: A sum of Rs.
1,25,00,000/-  (Rupees  One  Crore  and  Twenty-Five  Lakhs  only)
presently lying deposited with the Registry of the Hon'ble Supreme
Court of India in the SLP, shall be appropriated towards the
Settlement Amount. The Parties shall jointly move/file appropriate
application(s) before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India for release
of the said amount, together with accrued interest, if any, in
favour of the Bank, and the Borrower shall render full co-operation
in the said behalf;
b) Payment on Execution: A further sum of Rs. 35,00,000/- (Rupees
Thirty Five Lakhs only) shall be paid by the Borrower to the Bank
simultaneously with and on the date of execution of this Deed of
Settlement, by way of demand draft.
c) Balance Payment: The entire balance of the Settlement Amount, after
appropriating the amounts referred to in sub-clauses (a) and (b)
above, shall be paid by the Borrower to the Bank within sixty (60)
days from the date of execution of this Deed, by way of demand draft
/ RTGS / NEFT to the designated account of the Bank;
d) Grace Period: By way of indulgence and without prejudice to its
rights, the Bank agrees to grant the Borrower a further grace period
of thirty (30) days beyond the period stipulated in sub-clause (c)

--- Page 206 ---
4
above for making the balance payment, without attracting any default
consequence under Clause 5 below; provided that no further extension
of time shall be granted save with the express written consent of
the Bank.
2.2 Time is and shall be of the essence in respect of the payment
obligations contained in this Clause 2.
2.3 Each payment shall be deemed to have been made only on the date of
unconditional credit of the said amount in the designated account of
the Bank.
3. RELEASE OF SECURITIES AND RETURN OF TITLE DEEDS  
3.1 Upon receipt of the entire Settlement Amount in terms of Clause 2 above
(including the appropriation of the Supreme Court deposit and clear
receipt of the balance payment), the Bank shall, within a period of
fifteen (15) working days:
a. return  the  original  title  documents  in  respect  of  the
secured/mortgaged  property  to  the  Borrower  against  due
acknowledgement;
4. WITHDRAWAL OF PROCEEDINGS / DISPOSAL ON SETTLEMENT  
4.1 Upon the receipt of the entire Settlement Amount in terms of Clause 2
above, the Parties shall jointly take steps to:
a. place this Deed of Settlement on record before the Hon'ble Supreme
Court of India and pray for disposal of S.L.P. (Civil) No. 24286 of
2025 in terms of this Settlement;
b. close, withdraw and/or have disposed of, as the case may be, all
proceedings between the Parties pending before any court, tribunal
or authority arising out of or in connection with the said loan
facility, including but not limited to the proceedings in S.A. No.
425 of 2019, I.A. No. 885 of 2023, Misc. Appeal No. 35 of 2023, W.P.
No. 22458 of 2024, complaints/cases under the Negotiable Instruments
Act,  1881  in  respect  of  the  dishonoured  cheques,  and  any
application(s) under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, all of which
shall be withdrawn / treated as not pressed / disposed of in terms
of this Settlement; and
c. execute  such  joint  memos,  consent  applications,  no-objections,
releases and other documents as may be necessary to give effect to
this Clause 4.
4.2 Each Party shall bear its own costs of the legal proceedings and the
mediation costs shall be borne in terms of Clause 11 below.
5. CONSEQUENCES OF DEFAULT  
5.1 In the event of failure of the Borrower to pay the balance of the
Settlement Amount within the period stipulated in Clause 2.1(c), as
extended by the grace period stipulated in Clause 2.1(d) above (the
“Outer Date”), this Settlement shall, at the option of the Bank
exercisable by written notice, stand revoked, and the Bank shall be
entitled to:

--- Page 207 ---
5
a. appropriate any amount(s) already received under this Settlement
(including the amounts referred to in Clauses 2.1(a) and 2.1(b))
towards the outstanding contractual dues, without prejudice to its
rights to claim the balance;
b. revive and continue all proceedings referred to in Clause 4 above as
if this Settlement had not been entered into; and
c. pursue all remedies available to it in law, including under the
SARFAESI Act and the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993, on
the basis of the original contractual rate of interest of 13.5% per
annum compounded monthly together with penal interest of 2% per
annum, without any reduction or concession.
5.2 The Borrower expressly acknowledges that the reduced figure of the
Settlement Amount has been agreed solely as a measure of compromise and
on the strict condition of timely payment, and shall not, in the event
of default, be construed as the determined liability of the Borrower.
6. MUTUAL RELEASES, DISCHARGE AND NO FURTHER CLAIMS  
6.1 Subject to and contingent upon receipt of the entire Settlement Amount
by  the  Bank  in  terms  of  Clause  2  above,  each  Party  hereby
unconditionally  and  irrevocably  releases,  discharges  and  forever
exonerates  the other  Party (and,  in the  case of  the Bank,  its
directors, officers, employees, agents and representatives) from any
and all claims, demands, actions, causes of action, suits, debts, dues,
accounts,  reckonings,  bonds,  covenants,  contracts,  controversies,
agreements, promises, damages, judgments, executions, expenses and
liabilities whatsoever, whether known or unknown, present or future,
arising out of or in any manner connected with the Disputes.
6.2 The  Parties  confirm  that,  save  and  except  for  the  rights  and
obligations expressly created under this Deed, no claim, demand or
grievance whatsoever exists or shall be raised by either Party against
the other arising out of or in connection with the Disputes.
7. CONFIDENTIALITY  
7.1 The Parties, the Ld. Mediator and all participants to the mediation
shall maintain strict confidentiality of the mediation proceedings in
terms of Section 22 of the Mediation Act, 2023, including but not
limited  to  acknowledgements,  opinions,  suggestions,  proposals,
admissions  and  documents  prepared  solely  for  the  conduct  of  the
mediation.
7.2 Notwithstanding the foregoing, this Deed of Settlement may be disclosed
to the extent necessary for its registration, enforcement or challenge
under the Mediation Act, 2023, and for placing the same on record
before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India and any other forum referred
to in Clause 4 above.
8. TERMINATION OF MEDIATION PROCEEDINGS  
8.1 The Parties record that, upon the signing of this Deed of Settlement
and  authentication  thereof  by  the  Ld.  Mediator,  the  mediation
proceedings between the Parties shall stand terminated in accordance
with Section 24(a) of the Mediation Act, 2023.

9.2 The Parties acknowledge and agree that this Deed of Settlement, upon

9.3 The Parties may, at their option and within the period prescribed under

ENTIRE AGREEMENT, AMENDMENT AND SEVERABILITY

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Pursuant  to  our  judgment  dated
09.07.2018, the Government of NCTE of Delhi

--- Page 228 ---
6
filed the compliance reports. Thereafter, on
21.01.2006,  we  directed  the  Government  of
NCTE of Delhi to take action against the
erring hospitals who have failed to comply
with our order dated 09.07.2018.
2. Thereafter,  fresh  compliance
affidavit(s) was filed by the Government of
NCTE of Delhi enlisting the hospitals who
fall short in complying with this Court's
order dated 09.07.2018.
3. On 24.02.2026, we issued notice to the
hospitals  mentioned  in  paragraph-6  of  our
order as to why proceedings  should not be
taken against them for committing contempt of
Court for violating this Court's order; and
why the concessions granted to them by the
Government shall not be withdrawn.
4. The hospitals, to which notices were
issued  by  this  Court,  submitted  their
compliance  affidavits  upon  which,  we
appointed  Mr.  Sanjay  Jain,  learned  senior
counsel and Mr. Ninad Laud, learned counsel
as  Amicus Curiae  to compile and prepare a
chart  on  the  basis  of  the  compliance
affidavits filed by the hospitals.
5. A report was filed by the learned Amici
on 10.05.2026. In view of the report of the

--- Page 229 ---
7
learned Amici, this Court, vide order dated
13.05.2026, requested the learned  Amici, to
convene  a  joint  meeting  of  the  following
stakeholders/ officers;
a. The  amici,  Shri  Sanjay  Jain,
Senior Advocate and Shri Ninad Laud,
Advocate.
 
b.  Dr.  Kusum  Arora,  Superintendent
Nursing  Home  and  EWS  (Economically
Weaker Section) In-charge, GNCTD.
 
c.  Noticee  hospitals  through  their
medical  superintendent/authorised
officers.
d.  Secretary  of  the  Department  of
Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW), GNCTD.
e.  Director,  Land  and  Development
Office, Government of India.
f. Senior Officers from the land owning
agencies. 
g. Deputy Commissioner level officer
from Municipal Corporation of Delhi,
New Delhi Municipal Council and Delhi
Cantonment  Board.  h.  Director  level
officer  from  Delhi  Development
Authority. 
i. Joint Secretary, Ministry of Health,
Central Government.
6. After holding a meeting on 23.05.2026,
as ordered by this Court, the learned Amici
has filed an SOP titled as  “Delhi EWS Free
Treatment Standard Operating Procedure, 2026”.

--- Page 230 ---
8
7. Learned  senior  counsel  and  learned
counsel appearing for the noticee hospitals
would submit that the copy of the said SOP has
been supplied to them only a day before i.e.
on 27.07.2026 and therefore, they need time to
peruse the SOP and suggest improvements, if
required, so that after this Court adopts the
SOP, it should be properly implemented.
8. Having  heard  learned  amici;  learned
senior counsels and learned counsel appearing
for the parties, we feel that the SOP should
also dwell on the provisions/ procedures to be
taken for admitting emergency patients as soon
as  any  such  patient  is  brought  to  the
hospital.
9. At  this  stage,  learned  Amici,  would
refer to Clause-7 of the SOP which speaks
about  “verification  at  the  hospitals  and
emergencies”. Clauses 7.2 and 7.3 of the SOP
in particular, deal with the procedure to be
adopted by the hospitals when emergency EWS
patients are brought to the hospitals. Clause-
20 of the SOP which deals with the denial
protocol  and  Clause-20.5  thereof,  provides
that a hospital shall not be permitted to deny
treatment  to  an  EWS  patient  requiring  an

--- Page 231 ---
9
emergency treatment only on the ground that
he/ she has exhausted the EWS quota for the
Month.
10. Let  a  revised  SOP  be  filed,
especially dealing with the procedure to be
followed or is followed as to the emergency
treatment  required  by  the  EWS  patients.
Suggestions on this particular aspect, as also
on the SOP already filed by the learned Amici,
by the noticee hospitals shall be submitted
to the learned  Amici  within two weeks from
today.  Thereafter, revised SOP to the above
effect shall be filed by the learned  Amici
within the next one week.
11. Learned  Amici,  would  state  that
Yatharth Hospital, Dwarka (Noticee no.32)  has
neither attended the meeting on 23.05.2026 nor
responded to the notice issued by this Court.
12. Let  notice  be  issued  to  the
Yatharth Hospital, Dwarka explaining as to why
proceedings for committing contempt of Court
may  not  be  initiated  against  it  and  the
responsible  representative/  medical
superintendent of the said hospital may not be
sent behind bars. The medical superintendent
of the Yatharth Hospital, Dwarka, shall remain
in attendance before the Court on the next

--- Page 232 ---
10
date of hearing. Notice to this effect be
served on the Medical Superintendent of the
Yatharth  Hospital,  Dwarka  through  the

“COUNTER AFFIDAVIT ON BEHALF OF THE RESPONDENT No.2 &

and  vide  Order  dated  14.11.2024  the  impleadment
application No. 241034 of 2024 was allowed and Food

3. That the deponent has read the contents of the
present Writ Petition under reply and I say that the
petition seeks the implementation of clear Front-of-
Pack Warning Labels on packaged food products to
indicate levels of sugars, salt and saturated fats.
4. That the Food Safety and Standards Authority of
India (hereinafter 'Authority') is the statutory body
established under Section 4 of the Food Safety and
Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter 'FSSA, 2006'), an act
promulgated  by  the  Parliament  in  2006  for
consolidating  laws  relating  to  food  and  setting
science-based  standards  for  food  articles,  and
regulating their manufacture, storage, distribution,
sale and import. The applicant is also entrusted with
the function of ensuring availability of safe and
wholesome food fit for human consumption and for
dealing with any other matters connected therewith or
incidental to food safety. The Preamble of the Act
reads as under:
"An Act to consolidate the laws relating to food and
to establish the Food Safety and Standards Authority
of India for laying down science based standards for
articles of food and to regulate their manufacture,
storage, distribution, sale and import, to ensure
availability of safe and wholesome food for human
consumption and for matters connected therewith or
incidental thereto."
5. That Section 16 of the FSSA, 2006 specifies the
duties and functions entrusted with the aforementioned
Authority. That Section 16 (1) of the FSSA, 2006 binds
the FSSAI to regulate and monitor the distribution and
sale of food to ensure public health and safety While,
Section 16(2) empowers the Authority to set standards
3

--- Page 236 ---
and  guidelines  in  relation  to  food  articles,
specifying  the  system  for  enforcement  of  such
standards, as well as the food labelling standards.
6. That implementation of food labelling standards
including claims on health, nutrition, special dietary
uses and food category systems for foods falls within
the regulatory domain of FSSAI under Section 16 (2)
(h) of FSS Act, 2006 and regulation namely Food Safety
and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations,
2020 which was notified on 17.11.2020.
7.  It  is  submitted  that  FSSAI  has  proactively
undertaken  measures  to  implement  Front-of-Pack
Nutrition Labelling requirements and an amended draft
was notified on 13.09.2022 in exercise of the powers
conferred by clause (k) of sub-section (2) of section
92 read with clause (h) of sub-section (2) of section
16 and section 23 of the Food Safety and Standards
Act, 2006 (34 of 2006) and made available to the
public for objections and suggestions, to the proposed
amendment  in  the  FSS  (Labelling  and  Display)
Regulations, 2020, which include the proposed Indian
Nutrition Rating (INR) for FOPNL. This format is in
line with global practices and adopts a star-rating
system that presents simplified nutrition information
on the front-of-pack of pre-packaged foods and provide
information on the overall nutritional value of the
food and/or on nutrients included in the FOPNL". It is
designed to provide consumers with simplified, easy-
to-understand  information  on  nutritional  content,
assisting them in making healthier dietary choices.
8.  It  is  submitted  that  the  INR  system  uses  a
straightforward, star-based rating scale from 0.5 to 5
stars,  where  a  higher  star  rating  indicates  a
healthier product. This design aims to simplify the
complex  nutritional  content  of  packaged  foods,
enabling consumers to assess products at a glance and
encouraging healthier dietary decisions. By presenting
the rating on the front of packages, INR allows
consumers  to  compare  the  nutritional  quality  of
similar products easily, fostering transparency and
accessibility. The rating is based on factors such as
energy  content,  sugar,  salt,  saturated  fats  and
beneficial components like protein, fiber and certain
vitamins and minerals. The INR model integrates both
critical nutrients (such as added sugars, sodium, and
saturated  fats)  and  positive  components  (like
fiber,protein, and certain legumes and nuts) in its
scoring system. This balanced approach helps consumers
understand the over-all healthiness of a product,
rather than focusing solely on its negative aspects.
The  inclusion  of  positive  nutrients,  however,  is
regulated through caps to prevent nutritionally poor
4

--- Page 237 ---
products  from  receiving  disproportionately  high
ratings  simply  due  to  small  amounts  of  positive
ingredients. This structure ensures that the rating
accurately reflects the product's true health impact,
preventing any potential manipulation of ratings.
A true copy of Draft notification dated 13.09.2022 is
annexed herewith and marked as Annexure A.
9. It is submitted that over 14,000 comments were
received from the public stakeholders, including Food

regulatory  bodies  as  objections  and  suggestions
against  the  draft  amendment  notification  dated
13.09.2022.
10. It is submitted that to analyse and address the
robust  public  feedback  on  the  draft  amendment
notification, FSSAI
 constituted an Expert Committee on 17th February
2023. This committee, comprising of experts involved
with  FSSAI  in  developing  FOPNL  over  the  years,
conducted five meetings and carefully reviewed all
stakeholders comments. The expert committee in its 5th
meeting has prepared the report of its recommendation.
The report of the expert committee and the amended
final  (draft)  notification  of  FSS  (Labelling  and
Display) Amendment Regulations, 2022 will be submitted
to the Scientific Committee for further recommendation
and approval. A true copy of Constitution of Expert
Committee dated 17.02.2023 and subsequent extension
dated 30.10.2023 are annexed herewith and marked as
Annexure В.

and proposal will be placed before the Food Authority
for final approval.”

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
INTERLOCUTORY APPLICATION NO. 217445 OF 2026
 IN
TRANSFER PETITION (CIVIL) NO.3008 OF 2025
  MADHUREE RAUSA @ MADHURI RAUSA                    PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
RAJAT MAVI                                         RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. A joint application being I.A. No.217445 of 2026 seeking
appropriate directions under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India for dissolving their marriage by way of mutual consent as
per the terms of the Settlement Deed dated 26.07.2026, arrived
at between the parties, has been filed.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused
the material available on record.
3. Learned counsel for the parties submitted that all the
disputes and differences between the parties have been amicably
resolved, and the parties have decided to part ways on certain
terms and conditions. Accordingly, appropriate and necessary
orders may be passed in accordance therewith.
1

--- Page 264 ---
4. We appreciate the efforts put in by  learned counsel for
the parties in helping the parties arrive at an amicable
settlement. 
5. It is further agreed between the parties that, as per
paragraph no.3 of the Joint Application, the cases mentioned
therein, as described below, shall stand closed:
“(a)  FIR  No.19/2025,  registered  at  PS
Lashkar, District Pune City under Section
78 and 3(5) of BNS.
(b) FIR No. 0952/2025 registered at PS
Hadapsar,  Pune  City  u/s  85,75,
352,351,3(5) of BNS.
(c) Complaint Case No. 91401/2025 for the
offence  punishable  under  sections
318(4),322,316,61,314,303,109  and  123
BNS, 2023.
(d) Divorce petition bearing matrimonial
case no.962 of 2025 u/s 13(1) (ia)(ib) of
the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 titled as
“Rajat Mavi vs. Madhuri” which is pending
before  the  Ld.  Principal  Judge  Family
Court,  Gautam  Buddha  Nagar,  Uttar
Pradesh.”
6. The  terms  and  conditions  of  the  Settlement  Deed  dated
26.07.2026 are as under:
“1.  That  the  Parties  confirm  and
acknowledge that it is not possible for the
First Party and the Second Party to live
together as husband and wife and it has
been decided to amicably part ways and have
agreed that the marriage between them will
be dissolved by way of divorce by mutual
consent.
2. That Second Party has agreed to pay a
total sum of Rs.60,00,000/- (Rupees Sixty
Lakhs Only) to the First Party in addition
to the items handed over to the First Party
as mentioned in paragraph 5 herein towards
full and final settlement of all claims-
past, present or future - including but not
2

--- Page 265 ---
limited to maintenance, alimony, marriage
expenses, stridhan etc.
3. That the said amount shall be paid by
the Second Party to the First Party by way
of  a  Demand  Draft  No.  250615  of  Rs.
60,00,000/- (Rupees Sixty Lakhs Only) drawn
on Canara Bank in favor the First Party and
to be handed over to the First Party by the
Second Party during the course of hearing
before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India.
4. That in the consideration of the present
Settlement  the  First  Party  agrees  to
actively cooperate and extend full support
for quashing of the aforesaid FIRs before
the Hon'ble Court as the case may be,
including by filing appropriate affidavits,
joint application under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India for dissolution of
marriage  in  terms  of  the  present
Settlement, deposing before the competent
court in support of the quashing petition,
withdrawal etc. if required.
5. The Parties agree and acknowledge that,
apart from the Demand Draft mentioned in
Paragraph 3, all the jewellery, stridhan
and other articles belonging to the First
Party have already been returned to her at
the time of the execution of the present
Settlement deed and neither Party now has
any further claim of any nature whatsoever
with respect to the same.
6. That upon the compliance with all the
terms and conditions. mentioned here and
above and full payment of the settlement
consideration  as  detailed  above,  all
disputes,  common  differences  and
proceedings  between  the  Parties  whether
civil, criminal or otherwise arising off or
in connection with the subject matter of
the Settlement and the FIRs, shall stand
fully,  finally  and  irrevocably  settled.
Neither Party shall have any further claim,
demand  or  grievance  of  any  nature
whatsoever against the other Party and all
their respective family members, relatives
or associates.
7. That the Parties have not filed any
3

--- Page 266 ---
other  case/complaint/litigation  against
each other apart from the cases mentioned
above  and  undertake  not  to  file  any
complaint/ case against each other or their
family  members  in  future.  If  any  such
complaint/case  is  detected  at  a  later
stage,  the  Parties  to  this  Settlement
undertake to get the same quashed/withdrawn
in accordance with the present Settlement
and/or law.
8. That it is agreed between the Parties
that  after  signing  of  the  present
Settlement, there remains no claim of any
nature whatsoever for and against either of
the Parties towards each other or their
family members. All the matters, issues or
disputes arising out of the relationship
and all transactions between the Parties
shall stand settled fully and finally after
signing of the present Settlement.
9. That the Parties agree that there shall
be  a  total  severance  of  the  relations
between the Parties and they shall not
contact each other or their family members
in future.
10. That it is agreed between the Parties
that neither Party shall upload, publish,
share, circulate, or cause to be shared any
photograph, video, or other image of the
other Party or of the other Party's family
members  on  any  social  media  platform,
messaging application, or any other public
or  digital  platform  from  the  date  of
execution of this Settlement. The Parties
shall  further  remove/delete  any  such
photograph,  video,  or  other  material
already uploaded/shared/published etc. The
Parties further undertake to respect each
others' privacy and shall refrain from any
act that may violate this undertaking.
11. That the terms of the Settlement have
been duly explained and understood by the
Parties  and  there  is  no  scope  of  any
ignorance about the same and the Parties
shall remain bound by the same. The Parties
have voluntarily agreed to settle their
disputes and this decision has been taken
after due consideration and without any
coercion,  undue  influence,  fraud  or
4

--- Page 267 ---
misrepresentation. The present Settlement
cannot  be  retracted  in  any  manner  or
circumstances  whatsoever  subject  to
fulfillment of the terms of this Settlement
by both the Parties.”
7. In view of the above, the following directions are
issued:
i) The marriage solemnized on 04.03.2024 between the
respondent-husband  and  petitioner-wife  is  hereby
dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual consent;
ii) All  the  legal  proceedings  pending  inter  se the
parties, as indicated above, shall stand closed;
iii) Decree be drawn up accordingly;
iv) It  goes  without  saying  that  both  parties  will
continue  to  abide  by  the  terms  of  Memorandum  of
Settlement without any exception;
v) The Registry is directed to forward a copy of this
order to the fora/courts concerned for passing formal
orders closing the cases;
vi) The Settlement Deed dated 26.07.2026  is made part of
this order, and its terms are binding upon the parties.
Parties undertake to abide by the same; and
vii) Parties, through their learned counsel present in
the Court, have been made aware of the consequences of
breach  of  such  terms,  including  the  initiation  of
contempt proceedings.
8. In view of the above, I.A. No.217445 of 2026 is allowed
and the Transfer Petition stands disposed of.
5

--- Page 268 ---
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Disability Assessment Boards
1. Mr.  Senthil  Jagadeesan,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the intervenor points out that though the
Disability Assessment Boards have been increased from 33
to 62 as per the latest affidavit of the respondent No.1-
Union of India, there are no Disability Assessment Boards
in the following States:
a) Telangana
b) Madhya Pradesh
c) Odisha 
d) Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir
e) Union Territory of Ladakh
f) Meghalaya
g) Nagaland
h) Sikkim
2

--- Page 279 ---
i) Arunachal Pradesh
j) Puducherry
k) Andaman and Nicobar Islands and
l) Lakshadweep and Dadra and Nagar Haveli
2. Mr.  Vikramjit  Banerjee,  learned  Additional
Solicitor General appearing for respondent No.1-Union of
India submits that he will take instructions and come
back to this Court by 11th August, 2026.
3. Learned  Additional  Solicitor  General  draws
attention to the letter dated 24 th July, 2026 where the
letters have gone from the Union Government with regard
to the States where there are no Disability Assessment
Boards.
4. However, learned senior counsel appearing for the
intervenor  points out  that even  this letter  is not
marked to each of the above-mentioned States where there
are no Disability Assessment Boards.
5. Learned Additional Solicitor General promises to
look into the matter and report by 11th August, 2026.
6. We make it clear that these directions are part of
the judgment of this Court.  We will again monitor this
matter on 11th August, 2026.  The Union of India may come
with proper instructions in this regard.
3

--- Page 280 ---
Requirement  of  a  medical  professional  or  a  health
professional.
7. With  regard  to  the  direction  regarding  the
Disability Assessment Boards including a doctor or a
health professional with disability, the Union of India
shall before the next date of hearing inform the Court,
by way of an affidavit, as to the composition of the
Disability Assessment Boards in the different States all
over the country.  The affidavit will also set out, if in
any Disability Assessment Board, there is no doctor or
health professional with disability, the reason as to why
there is this deficiency. Let an affidavit be placed on
record before 10th August, 2026.
Appellate Body
8. Insofar as the constitution of the Appellate Bodies
is concerned, the affidavit filed by the Union of India
discloses that an  Appellate Body has been constituted in
New Delhi. Learned senior counsel for the intervenor
submits that there should be an Appellate Body for each
of the zones.  The idea is to ensure that every candidate
wanting to exercise his/her appellate rights should have
a real and accessible remedy.  If there is difficulty in
setting  up  the  Appellate  Bodies  in  every  zone,  a
mechanism may be worked out where the Appellate Bodies
have circuit sittings in the zone.
4

--- Page 281 ---
9. Learned Additional Solicitor General additionally
invites  the attention  to para  19 of  the additional
affidavit dated 29th July, 2026 whereby the Union of India
suggested as follows:
”19.  It  is  therefore  most  respectfully
submitted that this Hon’ble Court may graciously
consider  permitting  suitably  designated
Disability Assessment Centres situated in various
States and Union Territories to also function as
Appellate Bodies, under the overall supervision
and regulatory framework of DGHS, so that the
appellate  mechanism  becomes  more  accessible,
equitable  and  effective  while  substantially
reducing hardship to PwBD candidates.”
10. We direct the Union of India to furnish a scheme to
effectuate this mechanism.  We will take a call once we
examine the same.
Enabling Units.
11. Insofar as setting up of Enabling Units in medical
colleges  is concerned,  the Union  of India  has sent
advisories and emails to the institutions.  
12. Mr.   Gauravh  Sharrma,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the respondent-National Medical Commission
submits that a Circular dated 27 th July, 2026 has been
issued with regard to the constitution of the Enabling
5

--- Page 282 ---
Units for persons with benchmark disabilities. Learned
senior counsel submits that the Circular has been sent to
all Deans/Principals of Medical Colleges.  The National
Medical Commission may issue a letter to each of the
medical colleges through their Dean/Principal and ask if
the directions in the Circular dated 27 th July, 2026 have
been complied.  The colleges may be told that adequate
response to the letter of the National Medical Commission
asking for compliance with the Circular of 27th July, 2026
ought to be sent.
13. We direct that in case any of the colleges do not
respond or do not follow the directions in terms of the
Circular dated 27 th July, 2026, a serious view will be
taken against the individual colleges.  The National
Medical Commission may file an affidavit in this regard
on or before 16th September, 2026.
14. Call this matter on 11th August, 2026 at 2.00 p.m.

directed against such judgment and order.
3. Appellant  figures  as  an  accused  in  FIR
No.11187006240779 of 2024 dated 02 nd December,
2024 registered at Police Station Lunawada, District
             Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.5564/2026    1

--- Page 290 ---
Mahisagar, Gujarat under Sections 65(a), 65(c), 81,
98(2) and 116-B of the Gujarat Prohibition Act, 1949
and under Sections 336(2), 336(3) and 340(2) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. 
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for
the parties.
5. Chargesheet has been filed It appears from the
counter-affidavit  that  the  appellant  has  joined
investigation  by  presenting  himself  before  the
investigating officer on 02 nd June, 2026,  in terms of
an  earlier  order  of  this  Court.  Charge-sheet  has
since been filed.
6. Having regard to the nature of allegations and
taking an overall view of the matter, we are of the
considered  opinion  that  the  appellant’s  custodial
interrogation is not necessary and that he may be
admitted to an order for grant of bail in anticipation
of arrest.
7. Accordingly,  we  set  aside  the  impugned
judgment and order.
             Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.5564/2026    2

--- Page 291 ---
8. It is directed that in the event of the appellant
being arrested, he shall be released on bail on terms
and conditions to be imposed by the trial court.
9. If  the  appellant’s  presence  is  required  for
further interrogation, the investigating officer will be
at  liberty  to  call  upon  the  appellant  to  appear
whereupon he shall do so by attending the police
station  failing which liberty is granted to bring any
such omission to the notice of the trial court and
seek cancellation of bail.
10. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or  promise,  dissuade  any  person  acquainted  with
the facts of the case from disclosing such facts to
any police officer or to the court.
11. We clarify that the observations made in this
order  and  grant  of  bail  to  the  appellant  in
anticipation of arrest will not be treated as findings
on the merits of the case.
12. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed  on  the

aforesaid terms.

GAJJALA YOGANAND                              Appellant(s)
                           VERSUS
M/S CATALYST TRUSTEESHIP LIMITED              Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. This  appeal  impugns  an  order  of  the  National
Company  Law  Appellate  Tribunal  (NCLAT)  dated
30.04.2016 whereby IA No.601/2025 in Company Appeal
(AT) (CH) (Ins) No.217/2025 was rejected. 
2. The appellant is a personal guarantor of credit
facility  availed  by  a  corporate  entity  named
Manjeera  Retail  Holdings  Pvt.  Ltd.  (for  short
’MRHPL’-CD). On failure of CD to repay its debt,
personal  insolvency  resolution  process  under
Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,
2016 (for short, ‘IBC’) was initiated against the
appellant by M/s Catalyst Trusteeship Limited (the
respondent) i.e., the assignee creditor. By Order
dated 11.03.2025, the National Company Law Tribunal
(for short, ‘NCLT’) had admitted the insolvency
resolution petition. Against the order of admission
of the petition, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins)
1

--- Page 320 ---
No.217 of 2025 was filed before NCLAT.
3. In that appeal, the appellant moved an application
for stay, which came to be rejected by the impugned
order. 
4. According to Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul, the learned
senior counsel appearing for the appellant, the
stay application was heard on 25.04.2025 and orders
were reserved. The impugned order rejecting the
stay application was passed on 30.04.2026. It is
submitted that while passing the impugned order,
NCLAT  had  failed  to  consider  multiple  key
submissions; such as, for the very same loan of
which the appellant was a personal guarantor, one
Manjeera Construction Ltd. (for short, ‘MCL’) was a
corporate guarantor; petition(s) under Section 7 of
IBC were filed both against MRHPL and MCL. On the
Section 7 petition against MRHPL, a resolution plan
was approved making a provision for the claim set
out by the creditors including the respondent who
were  paid  thereunder;  in  consequence,  the
respondent did not press its claim against MCL
i.e., the corporate guarantor. It is contended that
those developments indicated that there was no
justification to proceed in the personal insolvency
2

--- Page 321 ---
resolution process initiated against the appellant
by the respondent. The grievance of the appellant
is that all these aspects were not considered by
NCLAT while rejecting the stay application. 
5. Shri Krishnendu Datta, learned senior counsel who
appears for the respondent, submits that it is
incorrect to state that the respondent is paid off
completely; the dues payable to the respondent are
in excess of 60 crores as on date and as there was
no stay on the admission of the petition under
Section  95,  in  the  meantime,  resolution
professional has been appointed who has invited
claims, and claims in excess of 300 crores have
already been submitted. In such circumstances, it
is not a fit case where this Court should interfere
with the order rejecting the stay application.
6. We have accorded due consideration to the rival
submissions. What surprises us is the lack of
discussion in the impugned order regarding the
subsequent  developments  which  have  been  placed
before us. Perhaps the long period for which the
order was reserved, as stated, might be the reason
for those aspects escaping consideration in the
impugned order. Be that as it may, we do not wish
3

--- Page 322 ---
to elaborate on that. However, since we notice that
there is no consideration of all the above aspects
while rejecting the interim application, we deem it
appropriate to set aside the order of NCLAT and
restore the interim application (I.A. No.601 of
2025) on the file of the pending appeal for a fresh
consideration by NCLAT in accordance with law,
preferably, within one month from the date a copy
of this order is placed before NCLAT. 
7. The appeal is allowed in the above terms. The
impugned order dated 30.04.2026 passed on I.A.
No.601 of 2025 is set aside. I.A. No. 601 of 2025
shall stand restored on the file of Company Appeal
(AT) (CH) (Ins) No.217 of 2025 for being considered
and decided afresh before consideration of the main
appeal provided appeal is not decided already.
8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.      OF 2026
(@ SLP(C) No. 16530/2026)
STATE OF PUNJAB & ORS.          ... APPELLANTS
VERSUS
JAI BHUSHAN MALIK & ANR.           ... RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. This appeal is directed against interim order dated 17.03.2026
passed by the High Court 1  in an appeal under Section 37 of
the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (‘1996 Act’). 
3. Facts  giving  rise  to  the  filing  of  this  appeal  are  that  the
appellant filed an appeal under Section 37 of the 1996 Act
against the judgment dated 20.04.2024, by which objections
preferred by the appellant under Section 34 of the 1996 Act
were dismissed and the Award passed by the Arbitral Tribunal
was affirmed. The appeal was filed along with an application
seeking condonation of delay of 462 days in filing of the appeal.
1 The Punjab & Haryana High Court at Chandigarh
1

--- Page 326 ---
4. The High Court in the impugned order dated 17.03.2026 noted
that the appeal has been filed with a delay of 462 days after
implementation of the arbitral award. The High Court observed
that repeated filing of belated appeals after implementation of
the  arbitral  awards  indicates  some  malice  in  the  system
regarding possible collusion and connivance within the state
machinery. The High Court held that such conduct prima facie
reflects a calculative intent to obtain a seal of approval from
the court after conscious implementation of the arbitral award.
The High Court found the explanation furnished by the state
to  be  unsatisfactory  and  directed  the  Central  Bureau  of
Investigation (CBI) to conduct an inquiry and submit a report
within a period of three months and further directed that the
appeal be listed on 20.07.2026. Being aggrieved, the State has
filed this appeal.
5. Mr. Nidhesh Gupta,  learned senior counsel for the appellant
submitted that the power to issue a direction to the CBI to
conduct  an  investigation  has  to  be  exercised  sparingly,
cautiously  and  in  exceptional  situations.  It  is  further
submitted that no ground for directing investigation by the CBI
is made out. Our attention is also invited to a report submitted
2

--- Page 327 ---
by  four-member  committee  constituted  by  the  State
Government. In support of aforesaid submissions, reliance has
been placed on a decision of this Court2.
6. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent has
supported the order passed by the High Court.
7. We have considered the rival submissions. In pursuance of the
direction issued by the High Court, a four-member committee
was  constituted  by  the  State  Government.  The  said  four-
member committee after examining arbitration matters across
departments categorically found that there exists no deliberate
or conscious collusion between the departmental officers and
the contractors. The committee further found that the delay in
filing the appeals occasioned due to multi-layer approvals and
the amounts due under the award were released only through
execution or coercive procedures and not through voluntary
administrative decisions.
8. In view of the aforesaid report of the committee and the facts
and circumstances of the case, in our opinion no case for
investigation  by  the  CBI  in  the  matter  of  delayed  filing  of
appeals  under  Section  37  of  the  1996  Act  is  made  out.
2 Anant Thanur Karmuse v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.; (2023) 5 SCC 802
3

--- Page 328 ---
Therefore, the impugned order dated 17.03.2026 passed by the
High Court is set aside. 
9. The High Court shall consider the application for condonation
of  delay  and  in  case,  it  finds  that  sufficient  cause  for
condonation of delay in filing the appeal is made out, it shall
proceed to decide the appeal on merits. 
10. Accordingly, the appeal is disposed of. There shall be no order
as to costs.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.11497/2026)
With
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.11496/2026)
SHYAM LAL MEENA ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Abhishek Gupta, learned counsel for the
appellant; Mr. Kshitij Mittal, learned counsel for the respondent-
State of Rajasthan; and Mr. Yogesh Kumar Meena, learned counsel for
the de facto complainant-respondent No.2.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by orders dated 23.04.2026, passed by
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at Jaipur
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) whereby appellant’s bail
applications have been dismissed.
4. Appellant is an accused in FIR Nos.486/2022, and  210/2022
registered at Police Station Ramnagariya, Jaipur City (East), under
Sections 420, 406, 467, 468, 471 and 120-B and Sections 323, 341,
1

--- Page 336 ---
384, 420, 406, 120-B and 506  of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for
short, ‘IPC’) respectively.
5. Accusation against the appellant is that his father and grand-
mother along with other  Khatedars had sold land to a housing
society through a power of attorney holder. The housing society in
turn had sold the land to different purchasers. Grievance of the
purchasers is that despite payment of money, the plots of land in
question have not been handed over to them. He is accused of
forging documents to facilitate the fraud.
6. This Court  vide Order dated 23.06.2026, had issued notice
pursuant to which respondent No.1-State of Rajasthan has filed
counter affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the culpability
or otherwise of his father and grand-mother cannot be passed on to
the appellant. He submits that it is the housing society who has
cheated the purchasers and not the  Khatedars,  therefore, the
grievance of the purchasers is mis-directed.That apart, he has been
in custody since 04.11.2025. He submits that investigation is
complete and charge-sheet has been filed. However no charges have
been framed. Therefore, appellant may be enlarged on bail.
8. Learned State counsel has referred to the counter affidavit
filed by the State and asserts that considering the magnitude of
the crime, it will be premature to enlarge the appellant on bail at
this stage. He submits that appellant is a habitual offender and
has a number of criminal antecedents of similar nature.
9. Similar  is  the  submission  made  by  learned  counsel  for
respondent No.2 – the complainant. He has stated that appellant had
2

--- Page 337 ---
colluded with other accused persons to illegally prepare forged
documents. He has re-sold the land allegedly sold by his father and
grand-mother to the housing society. His role in the commission of
the offence is quite discernible. Therefore, appellant should not
be enlarged on bail.
10. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and on due
consideration, we are of the view that appellant deserves to be
enlarged on bail more particularly having regard to the period of
incarceration undergone and the fact that the alleged offences are
all magistrate triable. High Court, in our view, has gone deep into
the merits of the allegations against the appellant, which should
have been avoided.
11. Be that as it may, we set aside the impugned orders of the
High Court dated 23.04.2026 and direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the Trial Court within a maximum period of 7 days
from today whereafter the Trial Court shall enlarge the appellant
on bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
12. Appeals are accordingly allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

(UJJAL BHUYAN)

found on the mobile phone of the appellant.
FIR is delayed and there is no medical
corroboration. Besides, the appellant has no
previous  criminal  antecedents.  In  such
circumstances, it has been submitted that
the  appellant,  who  has  suffered
incarceration for a period of about one
year, is entitled to be released on bail
pending trial.
6. The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
2

--- Page 342 ---
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail.
7. Having regard to the facts of the case,
without expressing any opinion on the merits
thereof,  we  are  of  the  view  that  the
appellant is entitled to be released on bail
pending trial.
8. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant is set
aside.
9. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.

Leave granted.
The appellant seeks bail in connection with
FIR No.281/2020, dated 04.09.2020, registered at
Police Station Sangli City, District – Sangli, for
the offences punishable under Sections 307, 143,
147, 148 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860,
Sections 4 and 25 of the Arms Act, 1959, Sections
37(1), 37(3) and 135 of the Maharashtra Police
Act, 1951 and Sections 3(1)(ii), 3(2) and 3(4) of
the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act,
1999.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.

--- Page 351 ---
2
Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submits that only one out of 58 witnesses has been
examined  and  the  appellant  has  been  under
incarceration for a period of five years and nine
months.
Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  State
submits that the appellant has numerous criminal
antecedents.
 Though there are criminal antecedents against
the appellant, the fact remains that the trial is
proceeding at a slow pace. The appellant has been
under incarceration for five years and nine months
and only one out of 58 witnesses has been examined
so far. The reason given by the High Court that
the accused are responsible for the delay cannot
be a factor to deny bail to the appellant as the
appellant is languishing in jail for five years
and nine months. Suffice it is state that the
appellant has not dragged on the trial.

--- Page 352 ---
3
Considering the above, we are inclined to
grant bail to the appellant.
Accordingly, the impugned order is set aside
and the appellant is granted bail on terms and
conditions to the satisfaction of the concerned
Trial Court.
The appeal stands allowed accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(s)……………………. OF 2026
(@Special Leave Petition (Civil) No(s).13289 of 2026)
NITHEESH ABRAHAM & ANR.               ... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
LIBERTY VIDEOCON GENERAL INSURANCE
COMPANY LIMITED                       ... RESPONDENT(S)  
 
                
O R D E R
    Leave granted.
2. The present appeal arises out of the judgment dated
04.11.2024  passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Kerala  at
Ernakulam  in  MACA  No.  574  of  2021,  whereby  the
compensation  awarded  by  the  Motor  Accidents  Claims
Tribunal, Ernakulam, was enhanced from 8,34,900/- to₹
13,39,969/-.₹
3. The  factum  of  the  accident  dated  26.09.2018,
resulting in the death of the appellants’ mother, is not
in dispute. The negligence of the driver of the offending
scooter, the subsistence of a valid insurance policy, and
1

--- Page 356 ---
the possession of a valid driving licence by the driver
are also undisputed. Hence, liability stands fastened
upon the insurer.
4. The Tribunal had assessed the monthly income of the
deceased  at  10,000/-  and  awarded  compensation  of₹
8,34,900/-. The High Court re-fixed the monthly income₹
at  12,500/-  and,  by  applying  10%  towards  future₹
prospects  and  deducting  1/3rd  for  personal  expenses,
enhanced  the  compensation  by  3,75,100/-,  thereby₹
awarding a total of 13,39,969/-.₹
5. The  appellants  contended  that  the  deceased  was
earning 21,000/- per month and that the Courts below₹
erred  in  not  awarding  compensation  under  certain
conventional heads, particularly loss of consortium.
6. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the record, we are of the considered view that
the  compensation  requires  modification  to  a  limited
extent. While the High Court has correctly re-fixed the
income and applied the multiplier, the head of loss of
consortium has not been adequately accounted for.
2

--- Page 357 ---
7. In the interest of justice, we direct that a further
sum of 3,00,000/- (Rupees Three Lakhs only) be awarded₹
under the head of loss of consortium, over and above the
compensation  already  awarded  by  the  High  Court.
Accordingly,  the  total  compensation  payable  to  the
appellants shall stand enhanced to 16,39,969/- (Rupees₹
Sixteen Lakhs Thirty Nine Thousand Nine Hundred Sixty
Nine only), together with interest as awarded by the
Courts below.
8. The aforesaid sum of 3,00,000/- shall be paid by the₹
respondent  to  the  appellants  within  four  weeks  from
today. Failing such payment within the stipulated period,
the said amount shall carry interest @ 6% per annum from
the date of default until realization.
The appeal is disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
9. The respondent-insurer shall remit the aforesaid
enhanced amount directly into the bank accounts of the
appellants.  Learned  counsel  for  the  appellants  shall
forthwith furnish particulars of the bank accounts to the
learned counsel for the respondent. The remittance shall
3

--- Page 358 ---
be effected within four weeks from the date of receipt of
such particulars.
10. The period of delay, if any, in filing this appeal
shall stand excluded while computing interest.
11. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. The State of Tamil Nadu assails the order dated 18.12.2024 in
Criminal R.C. No. 1933 of 2024 and the order dated 12.06.2025 in
Criminal O.P. No. 9339 of 2025, passed by learned Judges of the
Madras High Court. By the order dated 18.12.2024, a learned Judge
discharged K. Vamadevan, accused No. 4 in CC No. 14 of 2021 on the
file of the Special Court for the cases under Prevention of
Corruption Act, Chennai, arising out of Crime No. 2 of 2016
registered by the PS: V&AC, CC-II, under Sections 13(1)(e) and
13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, read with Section
109 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. By the order dated 12.06.2025,
another learned Judge allowed the quash petition in Criminal OP No.
9339 of 2025 filed under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
1

--- Page 366 ---
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, by accused Nos. 1 to 3 therein, viz., K.
Jayaraman; his wife, Shanthi; and their son, J.S. Arun Keerthi, and
quashed CC No. 14 of 2021 on the file of the Special Court at
Chennai.
3. Accused No. 1, K. Jayaraman, worked as a Chief Engineer in the
Construction & Maintenance Wing of the Highways Department, while
accused No.4, K. Vamadevan, worked as a Draftsman in the said
department under the control and supervision of accused No.1, K.
Jayaraman, the Chief Engineer. Pertinent to note, K. Jayaraman
retired from the post on 31.12.2015. K. Vamadevan was engaged as a
manager in the company incorporated by K. Jayaraman.
4. Crime No. 2 of 2016 was registered against both of them and
the family members of K. Jayaraman under the provisions of the
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The check-period for the
purposes of the case was from 01.01.2007 to 31.01.2016. Statements
I to VII were drawn up for the check-period, whereupon it was
alleged that the disproportionate assets, in terms of percentage,
came to 12.12%, which was over and above the 10% tolerance
allowable under the rules.
5. The thrust of the accused’s case before the High Court was
with regard to 2 items in Statement III, viz., items 86 and 87,
which were properties sold during the check-period at a far higher
price than the cost of acquisition. The issue raised by the accused
2

--- Page 367 ---
before the High Court was as to how this sale consideration was to
be treated for the purpose of arriving at the disproportionate
assets value, in terms of percentage.
6. Though, the learned Judges of the High Court were inclined to
accept the stand taken by the accused in this regard and came up
with an independent quantification of the disproportionate assets
value in terms of percentage, we are of the opinion that there was
more to be said on the issue than what was baldly summed up by the
learned Judges. Having applied their own calculations, the learned
Judges came to the conclusion that the disproportionate assets
value in terms of percentage would be less than 10% (9.76%) and
benefit was extended to accused No. 4, K. Vamadevan, in the first
instance, by discharging him and, at the instance of the other
accused, by quashing the case altogether by way of the second
impugned order.
7. We would not like to venture into the merits of the matter as
has been done by the High court as it was for the Special Court,
which was already seized of the matter, to examine all these
issues. Suffice it to state that this was not the appropriate stage
for the learned Judges of the High Court to have brought closure to
the  matter  by  letting  off  the  accused,  based  on  their  own
understanding of how the statements ought to be drawn up for
calculating the disproportionate assets value as a percentage.
3

--- Page 368 ---
8. The impugned orders dated 18.12.2024 and 12.06.2025 are,
accordingly, set aside. In consequence, CC No. 14 of 2021 shall
stand restored to the file of the Special Court for the cases under
the Prevention of Corruption Act, Chennai, not only against accused
No. 1 to 3, viz., K. Jayaraman; his wife, Shanthi; and their son,
J.S. Arun Keerthi; but also accused No. 4, K. Vamadevan, as we have
set aside the discharge order passed in his favour. The Special
Court shall proceed to deal with the matter on its own merits and
in accordance with law expeditiously.
9. The appeals are allowed.
10. Pending applications shall stand disposed of.

 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(Crl.)No 12091/2026)
GOLAM MUSTAFA MONDAL @ ZAFAR               APPELLANT(S)
                           VERSUS
STATE OF WEST BENGAL                      RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R 
Leave granted.
 1. The present appeal arises from the judgment and
order dated 04.03.2025 passed by the Division Bench of
the High Court at Calcutta in C.R.A. (DB) No. 297 of
2024, titled “Golam Mostafa Mondal @ Zafar vs. State
of West Bengal”. By the said judgment, the High Court
dismissed the appeals preferred by the appellant(s)
and affirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by
the Learned Additional District & Sessions Judge,
Bench-I, City Sessions Court, Calcutta in Sessions
Case No. 63 of 2017. The appellant stands convicted
1

--- Page 371 ---
under Sections 366B, 370(2) and 120B of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 and sentenced to undergo rigorous
imprisonment for ten years with fines, the sentences
were directed to run concurrently.
2. Our  attention  is  invited  to  the  order  dated
02.04.2026 passed in C.A No. 1714/2026, etc. by the
coordinate Bench of this Court. Though the judgment of
conviction stands affirmed, however, considering the
attending facts and circumstances of the case and more
so, that the convict therein had already suffered a
sentence of eight years and three months, the sentence
as imposed by the trial court and affirmed by the High
Court was reduced from ten years to ‘as undergone’. In
the instant case, we also find no reason to differ
with such finding of fact adopted by the Court. 
3. In the instant case, the appellant has already
suffered actual incarceration for a period of more
than  eight  years.  Considering  all  the  attending
circumstances and the sentence already undergone by
the  appellant,  where  the  maximum  sentence  as
prescribed is ten years, we deem it appropriate to
reduce  the  sentence  to  ‘already  undergone’  while
maintaining the findings on conviction as well as the
amount of fine.
2

--- Page 372 ---
4. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in part.
Conviction as directed by the Trial Court and the High
Court is hereby maintained. However, the sentence is
reduced to ‘already undergone’. We do not modify the
sentence insofar as the fine is concerned.  Needless
to add, the fine has to be deposited by the appellant.
Subject to the aforesaid condition, the appellant
shall be released forthwith if not required in any
other case.
5. Registry shall forthwith communicate the order to
the Berhampore Central Correctional Home, Murshidabad.
6. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3627   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 11110/2026)
SHEIKH RIZWAN S/O SHEIKH MUJIB      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF MAHARASHTRA     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Maharashtra.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  is  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
09.05.2025 passed by the High Court of Bombay, Nagpur
Bench (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting
the regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.239/2017
registered  at  Police  Station-  Pachpaoli,  District-
Nagpur, Maharashtra under Sections 302, 307, 143, 144,
147, 148, 504 and 506-B of the Indian Penal Code,  1860
(for short, ‘IPC’) read with Section 149 of the said
Code as well as Section 135 of the Maharashtra Police
1

--- Page 376 ---
Act, Sections 4/25 of the Arms Act, 1959 and Sections
3(1)(ii), 3(2), 3(4) of the Maharashtra Control of
Organized Crime Act, 1999.
5. This Court vide order dated 02.06.2026 had issued
notice  pursuant  to  which  respondent-State  of
Maharashtra has filed counter affidavit.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
appellant was arrested in connection with the related
FIR on 17.08.2017 and has been in custody since then.
Trial is not progressing in a satisfactory manner.
Therefore, there is no possibility of conclusion of the
trial in the near future. In the meanwhile, two of the
co-accused have been granted bail by the High Court.
Therefore, there was no reason for the High Court to
deny bail to the appellant. He submits that appellant
may be granted bail.
7. On  the  other  hand,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State  of  Maharashtra,  referring  to  the
counter affidavit, submits that the delay in progress
of the trial is because of the conduct of the appellant
and the other accused. It is they who have sought
adjournments on several dates. That apart, appellant is
a history sheeter and there is possibility of him
committing further crime, if he is enlarged on bail. He
submits that prosecution proposes to examine only 20
2

--- Page 377 ---
witnesses, out of which 14 have already been examined.
Therefore, at this stage, appellant may not be enlarged
on bail.
8. Submission of learned counsel for the parties have
received the due consideration of the Court.
9. We feel that notwithstanding the submissions made
by  learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Maharashtra, appellant deserves to be enlarged on bail
for the following reasons:
(i) Appellant has been in custody for more than 09
years as of today.
(ii) Two of the co-accused have been enlarged on
bail by the High Court.
10. Insofar as the pruning of the list of witnesses and
conclusion of trial is concerned, we are of the view
that it is entirely upto the prosecution whether the
witnesses cited in the charge sheet should be examined
or not. At the same time, merely because the trial
needs to be expedited, there should not be any undue
pruning of the list of the witnesses which may affect
the case of the prosecution.
11. In the circumstances, we are of the view that an
early conclusion of the trial may not be possible.
12. Having regard to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 09.05.2025 passed by the High Court is set aside.
3

--- Page 378 ---
Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the concerned Trial Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions
as may be deemed appropriate. One of the conditions
which the Trial Court may impose upon the appellant is
that the appellant should appear before the Police
Station- Pachpaoli once in a fortnight at 11:00 AM to
mark his presence as an assurance that he has not
involved himself in any other offence. Appellant shall
also ensure that no unnecessary adjournment is sought
for on his behalf.
13. Subject  to  the  above,  the  Criminal  Appeal  is
allowed.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

03rd AUGUST, 2026.

to affirm the date of applicability of the cut
off date 01/04/2001 for amendment of pay scale
and  has  impliedly  overruled  the  aforesaid
judgments.
XLIII. Because the Hon'ble Court could not
persuaded to be convinced while dismissing the
present  special  appeal  filed  by  the  state
appellants and got persuaded by the judgments
rendered  in  the  cases  of  Ghanshyam  Singh
(supra), Anand Kumar Misra (supra), UP Van
Sankhyikiya Seva Sangh {supra} and Gopi Charan
Kanaujia (supra) which have been passed in the
circumstances as stated above as such could not
be cited and treated as a binding precedent and
keeping in view of the aforesaid facts the
impugned judgment is liable to be reviewed as
there are apparent on the face of records.
XLIV. Because the impugned judgment and order
dated  27/08/2025  and  corrected  vide  order
dated 15/10/2025 is liable to be reviewed as
such in the interest of justice the operation
and enforcement of the impugned judgment and
order dated 27/08/2025 and corrected vide order
dated 15/10/2025 is liable to be stayed during
the pendency of the review petition."
4. Instead of examining the matter on merits, the High Court
dismissed the Review Application on the ground of delay.
5. Having heard the learned counsel for the appellants and the
respondents, we are of the opinion that the contentions raised by
the appellant-State about the change in interpretation of the law
by virtue of the decision of this Court will have a direct bearing
on the main decision rendered by the High Court. We are of the
opinion that it is necessary for the High Court to examine this
issue in detail while considering the Review Petition.
 6. In view of the above, the Civil Appeal against the order
2

--- Page 387 ---
passed  by  the  High  Court  in  Civil  Misc.  Review  Application
Defective No. 100 of 2026 is allowed. The said Review Application
is restored to its original number. The High Court will now
consider the Review Application and decide the same after giving an
opportunity to all contesting parties. It is also made clear that
the appellants will be entitled to challenge the order in review as
well as the main order, if necessary and if so advised.
7. Pending disposal of the Review Application, the High Court may
not proceed in the contempt proceedings.  All contentions are kept
open for both the parties to raise and contest before the High
Court. 
8. With this observation, the Civil Appeals are disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.4392/2026
VINIT MALL ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. & ANR.  ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant takes exception to the Order dated 06.01.2026,
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (briefly the
‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejecting the bail application of the
appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Case  Crime  No.722  of  2024,
registered  at  Police  Station  Sahjanwa,  in  the  District  of
Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, under Sections 109, 115(2), 351(2), 352,
103 (1), 117(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for
short, ‘BNS’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that he and others had
assaulted the son of the informant who later on succumbed to his
injuries.
1

--- Page 402 ---
6. This Court vide Order dated 16.03.2026, had issued notice.
7. In the proceedings held on 15.07.2026, we called upon learned
counsel for the petitioner to place on record the deposition of the
material witnesses.
8. Mr. Arijeet Prasad, learned senior counsel for the appellant
submits that in terms of the aforesaid order, appellant has
submitted the deposition of the material witnesses. Referring to
the evidence of PW-9; the Doctor, he submits that 2 injuries were
found on the body of the deceased. While injury No.1 could have
been caused by an accident or being hit by a hard object, the
second injury could not have been caused by a sharp edged weapon.
According to the Doctor, the injury could have been caused by a
stick or by other blunt object. He submits that having regard to
the period of incarceration undergone by the appellant, he may be
enlarged on bail.
9. Learned State counsel submits that out of 24 witnesses,
evidence of 10 prosecution witnesses have been recorded including
the material witnesses. She submits that because of the group
assault on the deceased of which appellant was a member, the son of
the complainant lost his life.
10. Learned counsel for the informant on the other hand submits
that it is a case of gruesome murder with the role of the appellant
clearly discernible. Therefore, this Court may not enlarge the
appellant on bail.
11. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties have
received the due consideration of the Court.
12. We find that out of the 24 witnesses cited by the prosecution,
2

--- Page 403 ---
evidence of 10 witnesses have been recorded including evidence of
all  the  material  witnesses.  Appellant  is  in  custody  since
02.12.2024, for more than one and a half years as of now. In so
far, culpability or otherwise of the appellant is concerned, it
will be decided in the course of the trial. That being the
position, we are of the view that the appellant may be enlarged on
bail.
13. Accordingly, we direct that the appellant shall be produced
before the concerned Sessions Court within a maximum period of 7
days from today who shall, thereafter, enlarge the appellant on
bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
14. Consequently, we set aside the impugned order of the High

1. Abatement is set aside.
2. Delay condoned.
3. Applications for substitution to bring on record LRs. of
deceased sole appellant and respondent nos.3,15 and 16 are
allowed, subject to just exceptions.
4. The appellant(s) challenge the judgment and order dated
10.07.2012 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna in
First  Appeal  No.829  of  1977  titled  “ Radhika  Devi  vs.
Sachidanand Prasad & Ors.”
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we are of
the considered view that no case for interference is made out
by the appellant(s) who have assailed the judgment and decree
dated 10.07.2012 passed by the High Court, affirming the
judgment and decree dated 24.09.1977 passed by the Trial
Court in Title Suit No.188 of 1975/1 of 1977. 
1

--- Page 410 ---
6. The crucial issues which the Courts below were called
upon to answer was as to whether the original appellant
namely, Radhika Devi, was re-married in the year 1947 or
1974.  Concurrently the Courts have held that the marriage
took place in the year 1947 and not 1974.  As such, no rights
in the property would have accrued in favour of the appellant
enabling her to seek a declaration under Section 34 of the
Specific Relief Act. 
7. In view of above, we do not find any reason to interfere
with the impugned judgment and order dated 10.07.2012 passed
by the High Court. 
8. The appeal is dismissed.
9. All contentions qua the will are left open.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO. 8157 OF 2016
RAM LALIT  & ORS.                            APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                       RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R   
1. The appellants challenge the judgment and order dated
12.04.2016 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad in Sevice Bench No.1768 of 2004 titled “ Ram
Lalit & Ors. vs. Union of India”.
2. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we are
of the considered view that it would be in the interest of
justice as also the parties, that the matter be remanded
to the Central Administrative Tribunal, Lucknow Bench,
Lucknow for consideration of the appellants’ case afresh.
More so, in view of the material placed on record vide
application bearing I.A.No.202554/2026.
3. We notice that the Tribunal had simply rejected the
appellants’ application by referring to the response of
1

--- Page 418 ---
the respondents, wherein it was stated that the appellants
were gainfully engaged in an establishment not being run
under the control and supervision of the Railways.   Such
finding had no basis. The High Court, in an appeal
preferred by the appellants, has simply reiterated the
reasoning adopted by the Tribunal.
4. In this view of the matter, we quash and set aside the
impugned judgment and order dated 12.04.2016 in Special
Bench No. 1768/2004 passed by the High Court, and judgment
and  order  dated  26.05.2004  passed  by  the  Central
Administrative Tribunal, Lucknow Bench,  and remand the
matter to the Tribunal for fresh consideration.
5. We direct the parties to appear before the Tribunal
on 14th August, 2026.  The appellants undertake to place on
record all materials including the document placed vide
I.A.No.202554/2026 before the Tribunal within four weeks
thereafter. Liberty is granted to the parties to place on
record  all  additional  material  within  eight  weeks
thereafter.
6. We request the Tribunal to decide the matter afresh
within three months.
2

--- Page 419 ---
7. With the above observations, appeal stands disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.10918/2026
MOHD. AFZAAL ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and learned
counsel for the respondent-State.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 28.04.2026, passed by
the High Court of judicature at Allahabad (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter) rejecting the bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Case  Crime  No.272  of  2025,
registered at Police Station- Chhapar, District- Muzaffar Nagar,
under Sections 85, 115(2) and 109(1) of  the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that he, along with other
family  members,  including  co-accused  Sajid,  had  physically
assaulted the informant because of which she sustained multiple
1

--- Page 422 ---
injuries.
6. Appellant is in jail since 21.11.2025.
7. This Court  vide order dated 11.06.2026, had issued notice
pursuant to which State has filed counter affidavit to which
appellant has filed rejoinder affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the main
accused Sajid has been granted bail by the High Court v ide Order
dated 17.04.2026, which order has not been assailed by the State or
by the informant. Considering the above and the period of detention
undergone, learned counsel for the appellant submits that on the
principle of parity, appellant should be enlarged on bail.
09. Learned counsel for the State, on the other hand, has referred
to paragraph 7 of the counter affidavit and submits that the victim
had suffered multiple injuries including incise wound on her neck.
Therefore, at this stage, it may not be appropriate to enlarge the
appellant on bail.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on going
though the materials on record, we find that not only Sajid but
also another accused Mohd. Israr has been granted bail by the High
Court vide Order dated 20.05.2026.
11. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that Mohd. Israr is
the husband of the victim.
12. That being the position and on the principle of parity, we are
inclined to grant bail to the petitioner.
13. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order of the High Court
dated 28.04.2026 and direct that the appellant shall be produced
before the Trial Court within a maximum period of 7 days from today
2

--- Page 423 ---
whereafter the Trial Court shall enlarge the appellant on bail on
such terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
14. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
15. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.
......................J.
(UJJAL BHUYAN)
......................J.
(ATUL S. CHANDURKAR)
